passages.t: The priest looks, waits and looks again
passages.happening:
The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron. “When someone has a swelling or rash or bright spot on his skin that could become an infectious skin disease, he must be brought to Aaron the priest or to one of his sons” (verse 2).

The priest looks at it. If the hair in the spot has turned white and the sore seems deeper than the skin, “he must pronounce him unclean” (verse 3). If the signs are not clear, “the priest shall isolate the infected person for seven days” (verse 4). He looks again on the seventh day, and if need be waits seven days more (verse 5). If the sore has faded and not spread, “the priest shall pronounce him clean; it is a rash” (verse 6).

A long-standing disease with raw flesh is unclean (verses 9-11). But if the disease has covered the whole body and “it has all turned white, he is clean” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
These chapters exist because God lives in the middle of the camp. A holy God among people who fall ill, give birth and die raises a practical question: how does the camp stay fit for him to live in? This chapter answers for the skin.

The Hebrew word for the disease is tsara'at. Older English Bibles called it leprosy, following the old Greek translation. But it is not the illness doctors now call leprosy, Hansen's disease. The marks of that illness, numbness and the loss of feeling, are not what this chapter describes. The signs here are white patches, scaling, raw flesh and spreading. They fit several conditions. The same word is used later in the chapter for mildew in cloth. It names something that can be seen on a surface and that spreads. It is not one diagnosis.

The priest here is not a doctor. He gives no treatment and offers no cure. His task is to look and to say what he sees. The words ‘pronounce him unclean’ and ‘pronounce him clean’ run through the chapter, because the priest's word settled where a person stood in the community.

Notice how patient the law is. No one is put out of the camp at first glance. The priest looks, waits seven days, looks again, and may wait seven more. The rules are clear and the same for everyone. They guard the person as well as the people.

And notice what the chapter never says. It never calls the sick person a sinner. Unclean is not the same as sinful. It meant that for as long as the condition lasted the person could not come to the sanctuary.

The rule in verses 12 and 13 is surprising. A person white from head to foot is clean. The concern was raw, open, changing flesh, not simply looking unwell.
passages.later:
The Bible tells of several people with this disease, and they are a mixed company. Naaman was a foreign general and ‘a mighty man of valor’ (2 Kings 5:1). Four men with the disease sat at the gate of Samaria during a siege and became the bringers of good news (2 Kings 7:3-9).

When ten men with the disease met Jesus, “They stood at a distance” (Luke 17:12), as this law required. He said to them, “Go, show yourselves to the priests” (Luke 17:14). He sent them to the examination this chapter describes.
passages.asks: The law would not let a person be judged at a glance. Ask whether you decide about people on first sight, by how they look or what you have heard. And ask what it would mean to look, wait, and look again before you speak about someone.

passages.t: Boils, burns, the scalp and baldness
passages.happening:
The same care is applied to other cases. Where a boil has healed and a white swelling or reddish-white spot appears, the priest examines it (verses 18-23). So too where a burn has left a spot (verses 24-28). In each case, if it is deeper than the skin and the hair has turned white, the person is unclean. If it is not, he is kept apart for seven days and looked at again. If it has not spread, “it is only the scar from the boil, and the priest shall pronounce him clean” (verse 23).

An infection on the head or chin is examined in the same way (verses 29-37). Dull white spots are “a harmless rash that has broken out on the skin; the person is clean” (verse 39).

“Now if a man loses his hair and is bald, he is still clean” (verse 40). Only a reddish-white sore on a bald head needs to be examined (verses 42-44).
passages.hearers:
This is case law, written as a handbook for priests. Each paragraph opens with a situation: a boil, a burn, a sore on the head. Then it lists what to look for. Has the hair changed color? Is it deeper than the skin? Has it spread? The verbs come in a fixed order: examine, isolate, examine again, pronounce. That made the practice easy to learn and hard to bend.

Much of the passage is about saying what is not the disease. A scar is only a scar. A harmless rash is harmless. A bald head is just a bald head. The law takes care to clear people, and not only to find fault with their skin. A clear ruling that someone was clean guarded that person against a hasty judgment.

Verse 29 says ‘a man or woman’. The same rules and the same care apply to both.
passages.later:
Job was covered ‘with terrible boils from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head’ (Job 2:7). His friends were sure he must have sinned. The book of Job says they were wrong.

Jesus was asked about a man born blind, “who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” He answered, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned” (John 9:2-3).
passages.asks: The priest had to learn to tell a scar from a disease. Ask whether you treat people's old wounds as if they were present faults. And ask whether you are as ready to say that someone is in the clear as you are to say that something is wrong.

passages.happening:
“A diseased person must wear torn clothes and let his hair hang loose, and he must cover his mouth and cry out, ‘Unclean, unclean!’” (verse 45).

“As long as he has the infection, he remains unclean. He must live alone in a place outside the camp” (verse 46).
passages.hearers:
These two verses are heavy, and they were heavy to live.

Torn clothes and loose hair were the signs of mourning in Israel. People looked like that at a funeral. A person with this disease looked like a mourner, and in a way was one. Covering the mouth and calling out warned others not to touch him by accident. And ‘outside the camp’ meant life apart from family, from worship and from daily work, for as long as the disease lasted.

Three things should be noticed.

The separation was tied to the condition and not to the person. The verse says ‘as long as he has the infection’. It was not a sentence for life, and the next chapter is the ceremony for coming home.

The text gives no blame. It does not say why anyone falls ill.

And the reason lay in the camp's center, where God lived. The marks of this disease, flaking and wasting skin, looked like death. When Moses' sister Miriam was struck with it, Aaron begged that she should not be ‘like a stillborn infant’. The signs of death were kept away from the house of the living God.
passages.later:
Miriam was shut outside the camp for seven days, “and the people did not move on until she was brought in again” (Numbers 12:15). The whole nation waited for one woman.

A man with the disease came to Jesus and said, “If You are willing, You can make me clean.” And “Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man” (Mark 1:40-41). By the logic of this chapter, touching him should have made Jesus unclean. In the Gospel account the man was made clean.

The letter to the Hebrews says that Jesus ‘suffered outside the city gate’, and adds, “Therefore let us go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore” (Hebrews 13:12-13).
passages.hard:
Why would God's law send sick people out of the community?

It is a hard command to read, and it was hard to live under. Readers answer in several ways. Some stress the health of the camp. Keeping apart, waiting and burning spoiled cloth would have limited the spread of some infections, whatever people then understood about disease. Others, among them Jacob Milgrom and Gordon Wenham, think the reason is mainly a matter of meaning. Flaking, decaying skin looked like death, and the law kept the signs of death away from the sanctuary of the living God. Mary Douglas read such rules as a way of ordering the world into clear kinds.

What the chapter does not say matters as much. It never calls the sick person a sinner. It builds in patience, and a way back. The separation lasted only as long as the disease.

The Bible does tell of particular people on whom this disease came as a judgment, such as Miriam and King Uzziah (Numbers 12; 2 Chronicles 26). Those are stories about those people. The law in this chapter makes no such link for the cases it describes, and Jesus refused to treat suffering as proof of sin (John 9:3).

Israel's later history shows that being kept apart could harden into contempt. That is part of why it was so startling when Jesus touched such a man.

So this chapter must never be used to picture any ill or disabled person as cursed, or to keep anyone at a distance today. Every person, with any disability or illness, is made by God and is precious to him. No one is a mistake.

A word for anyone who has been made to feel unclean, by an illness, by your body or by your past. That is not what this book says of you. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Jesus went to the person the camp had put outside, and touched him. Ask who is kept at a distance where you live: by illness, by how they look, by what people fear. And ask what it would cost you to go to them.

passages.happening:
The same word is now used of things. If a garment of wool or linen, or anything of leather, has a green or red mark, it “must be shown to the priest” (verse 49). The priest shuts it away for seven days (verse 50).

If the mark has spread, “the article must be burned up” (verse 52). If it has not, the thing is washed and shut away seven more days (verse 54). If the mark fades after washing, the spoiled part is cut out (verse 56). If it disappears, the thing is washed again, “and it will be clean” (verse 58).

“This is the law concerning a mildew contamination in wool or linen fabric, weave, or knit, or any leather article, for pronouncing it clean or unclean” (verse 59).
passages.hearers:
It can seem odd to find mildew in the same chapter as skin disease. In Hebrew it is the same word. That is one more sign that the word does not name a single illness. It names a spreading mark on a surface, whether skin, cloth or leather.

The method is the same too: look, wait seven days, look again. The law does not have a garment destroyed in haste. It is washed and watched. Only cloth that goes on spoiling is burned. Where the mark fades, only the bad piece is cut away and the rest is kept.

A coat cannot sin. The fact that the same rules cover a coat shows, as plainly as anything in the book, that ‘unclean’ is not a word of blame.

The chapter ends with a summary, as many sections of Leviticus do. The word for ‘law’ is torah, instruction. This is practical teaching for ordinary life as well as rules for worship.
passages.later:
The next chapter carries the same word into houses, where it is found in the plaster and stones of a wall (Leviticus 14:33-53).

The New Testament uses a stained garment as a picture. Jude tells his readers to show mercy with care, ‘hating even the clothing stained by the flesh’ (Jude 1:23). The picture works because readers knew laws like these.
passages.asks: The law saved what could be saved and cut away only what was spoiled. Ask where you throw out the whole of something, a friendship, a church, a person, because part of it has gone wrong. And ask what in your own life needs to be cut out so that the rest can be kept.
